The Hairy Bittersweet (Glycymeris pilosa) is a bivalve mollusc found in temperate coastal waters, where field surveys have documented its life-history traits under local thermal conditions. Egg development in this species begins with the release of fertilised ova into the water column following spawning events. Newly hatched planktonic larvae emerge as lecithotrophic veligers, sustained solely by endogenous yolk reserves during the initial dispersal phase. The wet weight at birth of a newly released individual is extremely low, calculated at 0.000000058 grams [Wwb = 0.000000058 grams], reflecting the microscopic diameter of the egg capsule itself. This tiny initial mass places G. pilosa at the lower end of the size spectrum among glycymeridids. At a sustained water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the maximum reproductive output of a single mature female has been estimated from field spawning observations as one hundred thousand eggs released in a single day [Ri = one hundred thousand eggs released in a single day], a remarkably high fecundity that compensates for the substantial mortality experienced during the prolonged planktonic larval phase.

Larval development proceeds rapidly under optimal conditions, and the completion of the planktotrophic feeding stage culminates in larval metamorphosis, during which the veliger undergoes a pronounced body plan reorganisation. Upon settlement and attachment to a suitable substratum, the developing individual achieves the larval-juvenile transition when the shell attains a specific dimension. Field-collected recruits of Glycymeris pilosa show that this metamorphic event occurs at a shell length of 0.1 centimeters , a standardised measurement taken as the maximum dimension across the prodissoconch margin. At this point, the post-metamorphic juvenile, or spat, begins to assume the characteristic adult morphology. The transition from a planktonic to a benthic existence represents a critical demographic bottleneck, as substratum selection strongly influences subsequent survival and growth rates. Comparative studies with other glycymerid species indicate that a 0.1 cm shell length at metamorphosis is within the typical range for the genus, although slight variations may occur in response to local food availability during the veliger stage.

As the juvenile bivalve continues its benthic development and somatic growth, it eventually reaches a critical developmental milestone marking the onset of gametogenesis. In Glycymeris pilosa, puberty—defined here as the shell length at which gonadal tissue first becomes microscopically discernible—is reached at a shell length of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. This measurement is based on comparative morphological assessments relative to the congener G. glycymeris, where a proportional relationship between shell size and reproductive maturation has been well established. Achieving a shell length of 4 cm typically occurs after several growing seasons, depending on local food supply and thermal regime. Once this size threshold is crossed, the individual enters the reproductively active adult phase and begins to allocate resources toward egg and sperm production. The pubertal shell length of 4 cm represents roughly half the ultimate shell height observed in this species, a pattern that is consistent with the timing of maturity in many marine bivalves.

Sexually mature adults of Glycymeris pilosa can attain considerable dimensions over their lifespan, with the largest individuals recorded from shell middens and dredge samples exhibiting an ultimate shell height of 8.5 centimeters [Li = 8.5 centimeters]. This maximum recorded shell dimension is among the larger values reported for the genus and likely reflects a combination of genetic predisposition and favourable habitat conditions. The corresponding wet weight of a fully grown individual, including the mass of the calcareous shell and internal soft tissues, can reach 181.7 grams [Wwi = 181.7 grams]. The adult body mass is substantial enough to represent a significant biomass contribution within the benthic community. Comparative growth increment data suggest that shell accretion continues slowly even after sexual maturity is attained, with the most pronounced annual growth occurring during the warmer months. The ultimate shell height of 8.5 cm provides a useful benchmark for age estimation in field populations when combined with growth ring counts from the hinge plate.

The lifespan of Glycymeris pilosa is relatively extended for a bivalve of its size, with longevity studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions providing a clear picture of its potential duration. At a constant ambient temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 69 years [am = 69 years], an impressive figure that aligns with the slow growth and late maturation characteristic of the genus. This centenarian-like longevity is derived from mark-recapture data and validated by incremental shell growth analysis, which reveals a steady annual deposition of material in the shell matrix. The extended lifespan allows for repeated reproductive events over many decades, a life-history strategy that buffers against occasional recruitment failures. Notably, the same thermal regime of 21 °C that supports the maximum reproductive rate also appears to be optimal for long-term somatic maintenance. Field observations indicate that individuals older than five decades are rarely encountered, likely due to cumulative predation pressure and the energetic costs of repeated spawning, though the physiological potential clearly extends well beyond common ecological longevity in the wild.
